prompt: Match each property to a forecast or a commitment.

pairs.left: changes with new information every week

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend saying the median date as well as the 85% date?

choices.text: Because stakeholders only remember the earliest date
choices.why: Memory is not the reason.

choices.text: It shows the 85% date is not padded
choices.why: Right. There is a real chance of finishing earlier, and saying so builds trust.

choices.text: Because the median is the commitment
choices.why: A median is even odds; it is the worst date to commit to.

choices.text: Because the 85% date is often wrong
choices.why: It is wrong about one time in seven, by design.

prompt: A team says "probably the end of October", and the stakeholder writes 31 October into a plan. The team finishes on 6 November. What went wrong?

choices.text: The team was slower than its history
choices.why: Nothing says so; 6 November may sit inside its range.

choices.text: The stakeholder should not plan at all
choices.why: Planning is fine; the date needed its probability.

choices.text: The forecast should have been a single date
choices.why: A single date is how this misunderstanding starts.

choices.text: A forecast was heard as a commitment
choices.why: Right. Say the probability, the date it attaches to, and when it will be updated.

prompt: The sentence that turns a forecast from a promise into a process: we will ___ this every Monday.
What is wrong with a year-long roadmap of crisp bars on a timeline?

choices.text: It claims false certainty far out
choices.why: Right. Confidence falls with distance, and the picture hides it.

choices.text: Timelines are too hard to read
choices.why: They are easy to read, which is why they are believed.

choices.text: Bars should be drawn vertically
choices.why: Orientation is not the problem.

choices.text: Roadmaps should never mention dates
choices.why: Near work can carry forecast dates.

prompt: Match each column of a now-next-later roadmap to how it is forecast.

pairs.right: Monte Carlo from throughput, with dates
an order of magnitude from reference classes
no dates; the order is the commitment

prompt: Why does moving something from later to now displace something else?

choices.text: Because the roadmap has a fixed number of rows
choices.why: The limit is the team, not the drawing.

choices.text: Because later items are more important
choices.why: Order decides importance; this is about capacity.

choices.text: Now is limited by work in progress
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4's limit makes the trade visible.

choices.text: Because stakeholders must approve it
choices.why: Approval may be needed; the displacement happens regardless.

prompt: When does an item earn a date on an honest roadmap?

choices.text: When a stakeholder asks for one
choices.why: Asking does not make it forecastable.

choices.text: At the start of each year
choices.why: A calendar does not create knowledge.

choices.text: When it is estimated in points
choices.why: Points do not make a forecast, lesson 9.

choices.text: Once it is broken down enough to forecast
choices.why: Right. Dates are attached as confidence is earned.

prompt: A feature was planned as 20 items and finished as 26. By what percentage did it grow?
With 20% growth, growth.py's 85% date for 30 items is 9 November; without growth it is 1 November. How many days later is it?
Why does growth.py draw one rate of discovery per future instead of a new one each day?

choices.text: To make the program faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: A project is messy throughout, or it is not
choices.why: Right. Drawing daily would average the messiness away.

choices.text: Because growth only happens on the first day
choices.why: It happens as items are finished, every day.

choices.text: Because the Billing team's growth rate is known
choices.why: Its files cannot measure growth; the range is a guess.

prompt: With growth anywhere from 10% to 40%, the median-to-95th spread widened from eight days to fifteen. What does that show?

choices.text: Not knowing the growth rate is itself uncertainty
choices.why: Right. The simulation carries it honestly into the dates.

choices.text: The team works more slowly on growing work
choices.why: The pace is drawn from the same history.

choices.text: The program is less accurate with ranges
choices.why: A range is the accurate input when the rate is unknown.

choices.text: Growth always doubles the spread
choices.why: No such rule; it depends on the range.

prompt: How can a team measure its own scope growth?

choices.text: By asking each person how much work grew
choices.why: That is an estimate of a fact the board can record.

choices.text: From items.csv, which records it
choices.why: billing.py does not group items into features.

choices.text: By comparing story points before and after
choices.why: Points add a guess to a count.

choices.text: Planned items against items it took, per feature
choices.why: Right. Five or six past pieces of work give a range worth using.

prompt: Of scope, date and confidence, how many can be fixed at once?

choices.text: All three, with enough effort
choices.why: Effort cannot remove the uncertainty.

choices.text: Only one
choices.why: Two can be fixed; the third moves.

choices.text: Two
choices.why: Right. The third is what moves.

choices.text: None; all three always move
choices.why: Fixing two is exactly what the levers allow.

prompt: Marta needs to announce at the fair on 6 November. Which question does Bia answer with howmany.py?

choices.text: How much of her list fits by then
choices.why: Right. Fixed date and confidence; the scope moves.

choices.text: Which developer can work on the fair items
choices.why: The forecast is about the team, not people.

choices.text: How many story points the screen has
choices.why: Points do not enter the forecast.

choices.text: Whether the fair can be moved
choices.why: The fair is fixed by the outside world.

prompt: What did Bia avoid doing? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Padding the date with a secret buffer
choices.why: Right. Discovered the first time the team finished early.

choices.text: Saying yes to 6 November to end the conversation
choices.why: Right. That moves the risk to the team, paid for in evenings.

choices.text: Treating the forecast as the end of the conversation
choices.why: Right. It was the start; the decision about risk was Marta's.

choices.text: Offering options with different confidence
choices.why: That is what she did.

prompt: When no lever gives an acceptable outcome, what does the lesson say the useful conversation is about?

choices.text: Who will work weekends
choices.why: That trades the date for the people.

choices.text: What changes the system
choices.why: Right. Less in progress, a dependency removed, other work stopped.

choices.text: Adding people to the team at once
choices.why: Adding people late rarely helps; Brooks, and lesson 12.

choices.text: Re-estimating every item more carefully
choices.why: Better estimates do not change the work.

prompt: On a burn-up chart, the scope line rises faster than the finished line. What kind of conversation does that call for?

choices.text: A conversation about working faster
choices.why: No speed on existing items catches growing scope.

choices.text: None; it will settle by itself
choices.why: The date is receding every week it continues.

choices.text: A conversation about scope
choices.why: Right. The work is growing faster than it is being done.

choices.text: A conversation about the chart's colours
choices.why: The drawing is fine; the scope is the issue.

prompt: The 85% date moved later for three weeks in a row. What should the team do?

choices.text: Wait one more week to be sure
choices.why: Three in a row is already a signal.

choices.text: Stop publishing the forecast
choices.why: Hiding the drift hides the warning.

choices.text: Switch to estimates in points
choices.why: The method is fine; the system changed.

choices.text: Find what changed, and say so
choices.why: Right. Growth, throughput, a blocked item: name it in the week it moved.

prompt: Put a weekly re-forecast in order.
items: update the items left, including new ones found
report the new range and why it moved

prompt: Why does the lesson say trust in a forecast is built by the weeks it was updated?

choices.text: It moves honestly both ways
choices.why: Right. Earlier as readily as later.

choices.text: Because frequent updates hide mistakes
choices.why: They expose them early, which is the point.

choices.text: Because one right forecast is enough
choices.why: A single hit can be luck.

choices.text: Because the date never changes once trusted
choices.why: It keeps changing as the work does.

prompt: growth.py with 10% to 40% growth gives a median of 5 November and a 95th percentile of 20 November. How many days apart are they?
